content_units: Corolla 2016 Symptom Snapshot
Your pattern points most strongly to an   air-fuel or ignition issue that is worse during cold operation  , with the ECU sometimes correcting enough that the check-engine light turns off later.

The combination of   rough cold idle + intermittent CEL + worse fuel economy + weak uphill power   most often fits a   minor misfire, dirty airflow/throttle issue, or sensor/fuel-delivery problem   rather than something catastrophic.
Vehicle context used
-   2016 Toyota Corolla
- Spark plugs replaced    30,000 km ago
- No mention of overheating, hard starting, smoke, or oil consumption
Ranked Likely Causes
Rank   Likely cause   Why it fits your symptoms   Typical first check   Usual repair cost level

1     Weak ignition coil / intermittent misfire     Cold rough idle, occasional CEL, reduced power uphill, worse fuel economy all fit a light misfire even if plugs are not very old   Scan for stored/pending misfire codes; inspect coil data and misfire counters     Low to medium

2     Dirty throttle body / carbon buildup / idle air adaptation issue     Very common cause of rough cold idle and lazy throttle response; can also hurt economy   Inspect throttle body; check idle behavior cold vs warm     Low
3     MAF sensor dirty or slightly out of range     Bad airflow reading can enrich fueling, reduce power, and trigger intermittent CEL   Read live MAF values; inspect/clean sensor     Low

4     Vacuum leak or intake hose leak     Often worst when cold; causes unstable idle and lean corrections, sometimes with intermittent warning light   Smoke test; inspect PCV and intake ducting     Low to medium

5     Fuel injector dirty / uneven fuel delivery     Can cause rough idle, poorer economy, and weak load performance, especially if one cylinder is marginal   Fuel trim review; balance contribution; injector pattern/cleaning     Medium
6     Upstream air-fuel/O2 sensor aging     Can slowly worsen economy and drivability without being constantly bad enough to keep CEL on   Check sensor switching/response and fuel trims     Medium
7     PCV valve issue     Cheap part that can create idle instability and mixture issues   Inspect PCV flow and hose condition     Low

8     Partially restricted catalytic converter     Sluggish uphill acceleration fits; rough cold idle is less classic, so lower on list unless misfire has been present for a while   Check exhaust backpressure or compare upstream/downstream sensor behavior     High
First Diagnostic Steps a Mechanic Would Usually Do
A good mechanic would usually start with the fast, high-yield checks before replacing parts.
Step   Action   What to check   Expected result
1     Scan ECU     Stored, pending, and history codes; freeze-frame data   Find misfire, lean/rich, MAF, or sensor clues even if CEL is off
2     Read live data cold     STFT/LTFT, MAF reading, coolant temp, O2/A/F sensor behavior, idle speed   Identify lean leak, bad airflow reading, or sensor bias
3     Check misfire counters     Cylinder-specific counts during cold idle and light revving   Confirms whether one cylinder is weak
4     Inspect ignition system     Coil condition, plug condition/gap, oil in plug wells, connector fit   Finds common cold misfire causes
5     Inspect intake path     Air filter, intake hose cracks, loose clamps, vacuum leaks, PCV hoses   Finds unmetered-air issues
6     Inspect/clean throttle body and MAF     Carbon at throttle plate; contamination on MAF element   Often improves cold idle and response
7     Smoke test intake     Small leaks not visible by eye   Confirms vacuum leak if trims suggest lean operation
8     Fuel/exhaust follow-up if needed     Injector balance, fuel pressure, catalyst restriction   Used if basic checks are inconclusive
Low-Cost vs Higher-Cost Repairs
Usually lower-cost
These are the most common “start here” items:
-   Diagnostic scan and live-data review
-   Throttle body cleaning and idle relearn
-   MAF sensor cleaning   or replacement if clearly faulty
-   PCV valve replacement
-   Vacuum hose / intake boot repair
-   Single ignition coil replacement   if one cylinder is misfiring
-   Air filter replacement   if dirty
Usually medium-cost
-   Full set of ignition coils   if more than one is weak or aging
-   Fuel injector cleaning service
-   One or more injector replacements
-   Upstream air-fuel / O2 sensor replacement
-   Repeat spark plug service   only if wrong plugs were installed, gap is wrong, or plugs are fouled early
Usually higher-cost
-   Catalytic converter replacement
-   Fuel pump or fuel-pressure regulation repair
-   Major intake manifold leak repair
-   Compression-related engine work   if there is valve sealing or internal wear
Most Practical Diagnosis Order
If this were in a shop, the smartest order is usually:
1.   Scan for stored and pending codes
2.   Look at cold-start fuel trims and misfire counts
3.   Inspect coils, plugs, intake hose, and PCV
4.   Clean throttle body and check/clean MAF
5.   Smoke test for vacuum leaks
6.   Then move to injector, O2/A/F sensor, or catalytic converter checks if still unresolved
That order avoids expensive guessing and catches the most probable issues first.
Best-Guess Priority Call
If I had to rank the   most plausible real-world fixes   for your exact symptom set:
-   First suspect:   intermittent   coil-related misfire
-   Second suspect:     dirty throttle body / airflow issue
-   Third suspect:     MAF sensor contamination or vacuum leak
-   Fourth suspect:     injector imbalance
-   Fifth suspect:     aging upstream air-fuel sensor
-   Less likely but important if power loss gets worse:     catalytic converter restriction
